title: Iran Sends Formal Peace Terms to the White House Via Qatar, Seoul Refuses Troops for the US War, and the Houthis Strike Riyadh for the First Time Since the Escalation
subhead: Tehran lays out conditions to end the war — an end to fighting on all fronts and the lifting of the US naval blockade — via Qatari mediators, while South Korea publicly refuses to send military support for the US campaign and the Houthis fire a ballistic missile at the Saudi capital.

sections.heading: Iran Conveys Peace Conditions to Washington Through Qatari Mediators
sections.body:
Iran's top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, told Al Jazeera that Tehran has sent its conditions for ending the war to the White House through Qatari intermediaries. According to Al Jazeera's report, the demands include an end to the war on all fronts, the release of frozen Iranian assets, and the lifting of the US naval blockade on Iranian ports. Tehran says it is now awaiting President Trump's response.

This is the clearest public signal yet that Iran is prepared to negotiate an end to the conflict. The choice of Qatar as channel, the specificity of the preconditions, and the fact that Tehran aired the terms publicly suggest a calibrated bid to test Washington while positioning itself as the party seeking de-escalation. Whether the Trump administration engages, and on what basis, will now define the near-term trajectory of the war.
sections.whyItMatters: A formal, public statement of Tehran's terms via a trusted mediator marks a potential pivot from open-ended conflict toward negotiated off-ramps — but the preconditions, especially lifting the naval blockade, remain significant asks.

sections.heading: South Korea Refuses Troops for the US-Iran Campaign, Defying Trump Pressure
sections.body:
South Korea will not send military forces to support the US war on Iran, according to the Guardian, openly defying pressure from the Trump administration. The decision marks a notable break from Seoul's usual alignment with Washington on major security issues and comes as the US seeks burden-sharing from allies in the conflict.

The development is significant because South Korea hosts some of the largest US military deployments in the region and is a treaty ally. Its public refusal signals that the political cost of the Iran war is spreading beyond the battlefield, testing the cohesion of the US alliance network even among partners with deep security ties to Washington.
sections.whyItMatters: An established US treaty ally openly declining to contribute troops is a signal of eroding alliance consensus around the Iran campaign, not just in the Middle East but among core Pacific partners.

sections.heading: Houthis Fire on Riyadh for the First Time Since the Escalation; Turkey and Pakistan Rally to Saudi Defence
sections.body:
The Houthis said they targeted the Saudi capital with ballistic missiles, and the Saudi-led coalition reported it intercepted a missile aimed at Riyadh on Saturday. BBC and Al Jazeera reported a strike on a fuel depot near Riyadh airport caused delays — the first air raid alert in the capital since the escalation in the Houthi-Saudi war. The Houthis have also pressed territorial gains along the Red Sea coast, including toward the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.

In parallel, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan told broadcaster NTV that Saudi Arabia may have unmet military needs and that Turkiye would consider how to support the kingdom under a trilateral defence pact, adding it is unacceptable for Saudi Arabia to be dragged into the US-Iran war. Pakistan has made a similar pledge to defend Saudi Arabia under the same pact, according to a Pakistani military spokesperson quoted by Arab News.
sections.whyItMatters: A Houthi missile reaching Riyadh's airspace changes the risk calculus for Saudi Arabia and could draw it further into the wider conflict; the converging Turkish and Pakistani defence pledges show the Houthi war is increasingly regionalizing beyond Yemen.

sections.heading: Bombing Kills at Least 21 at a Pakistani Mosque; Trump Signs the Russia Sanctions Bill
sections.body:
At least 21 people were killed when a vehicle loaded with explosives rammed a mosque in northwest Pakistan, during which gunmen also opened fire on a police facility, with a four-year-old child among the dead, BBC reported. The attack is the latest in a series of recurrent bombings in the region that Al Jazeera described as a growing challenge for Pakistan's security forces.

Separately, President Trump signed the sweeping Russia sanctions bill that Congress passed this week, named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a prominent advocate of aid to Ukraine, BBC reported. The bill targets buyers of Russian oil and expands Washington's economic pressure on Moscow.
sections.whyItMatters: The mosque bombing underscores a persistent militant threat across Pakistan's northwest even as Islamabad deepens its defence commitments in the Gulf, while the signed Russia sanctions bill locks in a new layer of economic conflict with Moscow.

sections.heading: Cuba's Grid Collapses Again, Japan Raises Rates to a 31-Year High, and Germany Votes in Two States
sections.body:
Millions were left without power as Cuba suffered another nationwide blackout — at least the sixth this year — a crisis Al Jazeera and BBC attributed partly to fuel shortages worsened by the US energy blockade. In Japan, the central bank raised interest rates to a 31-year high to curb the impact of rising prices, the Guardian reported, a milestone in Japan's turn away from decades of ultra-loose policy.

In Germany, two states went to the polls on Sunday with the future of the chancellor and his coalition hanging in the balance, according to the Guardian, as record fuel prices across the EU prompted calls from some quarters for a bloc-wide windfall tax.
sections.whyItMatters: These developments mark distinct pressure points in the global economy and European politics: Cuba's cascading grid failures intensify a humanitarian and energy crisis under blockade, Japan's rate rise signals a global shift in monetary conditions, and Germany's state elections could reshuffle the domestic landscape of Europe's largest economy.

bottomLine: The day's defining shift is diplomatic: Tehran has publicly laid out terms to end the war through Qatari channels, and Seoul has openly refused US demands for troops — together signalling that the conflict is moving toward a negotiated phase even as the Houthi war spreads to Saudi Arabia's capital. The Houthi missile strike on Riyadh, Pakistan's devastating mosque bombing, and the signed Russia sanctions bill all underscore how the war's ripple effects and the wider competition for the global order continue to reshape regions from the Gulf to the Indo-Pacific to Europe. Whether Washington engages Iran's terms — and how Riyadh responds to a missile over its capital — will set the course of the next phase.
